utterances.text: So we have -- although a bit of a different character, we have a newspaper reporting -- at least that's what you say what was said from the Serb side. And then we have pages 2 and 3 reflecting the speeches from the other two parties at that same meeting. Madam Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D248, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse, D247 where it seems most important is the -- that these were maps presented by the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ in relation to the Cutileiro plan. These are maps with a lot of names in it. Some of the maps almost illegible, as far as the text is concerned. One of the agendas to the maps being cut off in part. And I wonder whether it would make such sense to have it translated. Most important seems to be the different shades of grey in this black and white document. So I suggest to the parties that there were two different maps with different, I would say, approaches to how the territory should be attributed to the different parties that it doesn't make that much sense to try to decipher all the text on it and -- but at least I'd like to invite Mr. Krajisnik to tell us which one of the maps was presented by which party. Could it be returned on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After that's been done, Your Honour, perhaps I could address the Chamber generally about the issue of translation of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that, for example, that document, to the best of my knowledge, we don't have. Certainly it wasn't given to us last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so. Mr. Krajisnik, there are three maps. The top one was presented by which party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one was presented by the Serb side, number 1 that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was presented by.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That one was presented by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the bottom one was presented by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the third by the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move to the top. I can identify more or less what says this is Serb, this is Muslim, and this -- should be Croatian. And then it seems that a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A specific -- that there seems to be one portion that I don't know what it is. Could you read the fourth box of the legenda. Madam Usher, you're moving it out now from the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read what the fourth box says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff of the UN, at the same time the centre of the new state. And this refers to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the Sarajevo area. Next, second map, please, could we move up so that -- yes. We see it's cut off, but at least we see that the first -- could you zoom in perhaps a little bit. It seems that what is in the first box is Serb. What we see in the second box seems to be Croatian. Is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the third box should then be Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether there's a fourth one, we do not know. But let's move up so we now see the last map. There we see only one box, and could we zoom in and could you please tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the Croats in presenting this map were more concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cantons. The Croatian cantons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that they were more interested in what should be Croatian rather than to express themselves on a further division between Muslims and/or -- Muslims and Serbs. Okay. That's clear. It could be returned to Mr. [sic] Registrar. The parties are invited to express themselves if they think there is any need to have this map at, quite some effort, be translated. Mr. Krajisnik, we've dealt with all the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to add a last sentence or is this what you wanted to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me the opportunity to present this. Within two days I shall submit a brief explanation, according to your instructions, along with the documents I have placed on the DVD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We look forward to receiving that. Mr. Stewart -- Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just about the translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All the documents that was submitted last week we have sent to the CLSS for translation. I seek some guidance from the Chamber as to what should happen about today's documents. Let me emphasise, of course, we don't have copies of many of these documents, to the best of my knowledge at least, those that have just been handed up, and in addition to that, of course, there are all these documents on the CD. Clearly the Chamber, the Prosecution, and indeed the Defence want them translated as expeditiously as possible. If Your Honour would prefer that I dealt with the matter behind the scenes, so to speak, with one of the Legal Officers and one of my learned friends. I'm happy to do that, but some guidance would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem for the Chamber at this moment is, Mr. Josse, that we do not know how much work it is. That's the reason why we invited Mr. Krajisnik to -- to put these documents in the order of priority. I take it that they'll be printed out so that we at least know what it is because it's very difficult to make an assessment on the basis of this. So what we need is, first of all, a printout of these documents as they appear on the CD. We then could identify perhaps already documents that are already there in translation. For example, if there is something from the Official Gazette, it could well it be that there is a translation already, so that should be the second step. Then first priority should be given to a translation of the -- of the index, as we have received it now, and we could start with that immediately so that we at least know how it is described. Then the next thing which is really urgent is that we have translated as soon as possible Mr. Krajisnik's list so that we know what he considers to be the content of these documents so that they are -- and also to know what the priority is because on the basis of the volume of the material and on the basis of the priority list of Mr. Krajisnik, we could make a schedule on further translations. And, as I already indicated, the interview with Mr. Karadzic which might be a vital matter to be discussed at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Statement, I'm sorry, yes, it's a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we could start with that already. As far as the -- let me just -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apart from the index, the short descriptions given by Mr. Krajisnik and the statement of Mr. Karadzic, we'll wait to give further instructions for translations -- or at least to ask further assistance by CLSS on the basis of what we will know the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about the third category of documents, those that Mr. Krajisnik has just handed up in the last ten minutes or so and have already been assigned numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, they should be considered in light of -- we know -- we have the three lines already for them. And the parties, as far as the maps are concerned, the parties could express themselves on whether they would even like to receive a translation or whether the picture is good enough. And for the remainder, I would very much consider that in relation or with the priority list of -- given by Mr. Krajisnik, you may have observed that what was said in Paris as to contradicting -- contradicting reports on the existence of camps might not -- might not have the highest priority for translation. So therefore, we would like to consider that also two days after today when we have received Mr. Krajisnik's list and when we have received the translation of the short descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask that Madam Registrar provide the parties with copies of the documents that Mr. Krajisnik has just handed up some time this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- Mr. -- Madam Registrar is invited to provide you with copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else? If not, then this concludes the examination-in-chief of you, Mr. Krajisnik. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to start its cross-examination, I'd first of all like to remind you -- not specifically because cross-examination is starting but just because I forgot this morning that what you told us this morning that you're bound, but I take it you've understood that by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You even referred to the fact that you're expected to tell us the truth, so we understand your testimony in that respect. Then I have a very practical procedural issue in relation to the exhibits which were introduced through Witness D24. We have D172A and D172B, that is the English and B/C/S versions of a letter from Mr. Krajisnik to Mr. Cutileiro. Whether it should have been 172 and 172.1 is still to be considered, but at least we have -- this letter is provisionally admitted, and if there are any objections we would like to hear from the Prosecution within the next three days. Then we have Prosecution exhibits 1165, that's a request for registration of news agency SRNA. We have P1167, an order signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, dated the 23rd of April, 1992; and P1169, a decision signed by Bogdan Subotic, 18th of April, 1992. These three exhibits are also provisionally admitted into evidence. If within three days there are no objections from the Defence, they'll become finally admitted. This being on the record, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can take care of the necessary logistics without need of any brief break, but in order to ensure that's the case I need to determine whether -- we will be referring to particularly the Assembly sessions of 1991, 1992, early 1993 I think with some frequency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have bundles of a lot of sessions on our desk. I wouldn't say it's a complete set, otherwise -- there's also this -- if we have clearly identified which Assembly session we are talking about, even if they have different numbers, it might not be necessary to always refer -- to refer to all the numbers. Choose the one from which you're working, and we'll then follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well. And I would ask that a set of those materials be made available to Mr. Krajisnik so he has them as we proceed in the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got only the English here, but is there a B/C/S set?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge we don't have the material in that form. I may be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I actually distributed those to Mr. Stewart in both English and B/C/S the -- some time back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you will find it. A B/C/S copy will be given to Madam Usher so that she always can present the document which we are focussing on at that time to Mr. Krajisnik. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition, Your Honour, there are bundles of materials which are appropriately tabbed which I'd like to have distributed to the Court and to the Defence and to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are not Assembly sessions, they are other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They're either other documents, Your Honour, or post -- they are Assembly sessions that are not contained in the four binders that have been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is additional material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there any chance we could have an extra copy, because otherwise only one counsel will -- thank you. Is this on its way? Am I stealing somebody else's right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know precise -- I don't know how many copies were prepared. Obviously if there is an extra copy, we're happy to provide you with two, but I don't know if logistics allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got two at the moment. So if nobody else is deprived currently, everything's already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Theft, missing matters, can be reported to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, over the past several weeks you've had an opportunity to respond to questions from your counsel, and I recognise that some of those questions were intended to provide you with an opportunity to tell as much as you could about the particular subject involved. During my examination, I will be focussing you on particular aspects of events in 1991, 1992, and the relevant periods of time. I will be asking you to listen carefully to my question and just respond to the question I ask, rather than use them as a point of departure for elaboration. If I want or the Court wants or if your counsel subsequently wants you to provide additional details about any aspect relating to those questions, you will then be asked. And I know you've had a chance to sit through cross-examination and understand that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the early part of your testimony, I think it was day two in fact, you indicated that in 1991 and 1992 the Muslims were the most numerous people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that indeed, due to the birth rate, they would relatively soon become an actual majority of 51 per cent rather than a relative majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was, in fact, concern among the deputies of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and among the Bosnian Serb leadership about the birth rate of Muslims- correct- in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not formulated all that well, but I did speak about it and I could confirm this if I were given a chance to explain further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me direct your attention by way of focussing that to certain comments and remarks and positions taken by Bosnian Serb deputies and Bosnian Serb leaders. First if I could ask you to turn to tab 2. And in particular, Mr. Krajisnik, if you could turn to the B/C/S at SA043638.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the English that would be page 12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is a different marking, 0103 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the usher will help -- will assist you. I think you're looking at an Assembly session --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me, could you just tell me the number and I'll find it right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: SA04-3638, page 12 of the English. Again, for the benefit of the usher, I think you're looking at the Assembly sessions which are in binders. I'd like you to look at the tab bundle that was provided. The usher now has it. It's to your right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately the last from the handwriting, the last three digits 638. 638, the last three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll see they are note taken at a 24 December 1991 meeting of the Bosnian Serb Political Council, and in particular the articles of Professor Najdanovic who you had occasion to mention during the course of your Professor Najdanovic said at the Political Council: We can split up on the basis of the recent census. What happens to Serbs in Croatia," and then he goes on. And his last two sentences are: "What are our maximum borders? We need a single Serbian state which cannot be inhabited by Muslims because they would overwhelm us with their birth rate." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that was an expression of concern about the perception that Muslims had a birth rate that would soon make them a majority population and the prospects that was understood to cause for Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim birth rate was certainly an element that caused concern for Serb deputies and other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at other reflections of that concern and the extent of that concern. You mention Goran Zekic a couple of times - a few times, I think, in your testimony - most recently on May 24 you recalled Mr. Deronjic's testimony, as you recalled it, that Mr. Deronjic considered him a major contact between the leadership and Mr. Deronjic. And before I turn you to Mr. Zekic's comment, that perception would be consistent with what Dr. Karadzic told the Bosnian Serb deputies on February 15th, 1992, at the 7th Assembly Session, and that can be found at page -- if you turn to the 7th Assembly Session, sir. That's in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to put this away now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be -- Mr. Krajisnik, we'll be moving back and forth, so keep all this material as handy as possible. There's no -- we'll be --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I need to redistribute for the benefit of the Court and, indeed, for Mr. Krajisnik the B/C/S translation. Apparently the one provided was for the stenogramme; this one is for the transcript which appears in the English portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The particular portion, Mr. Krajisnik, is found at page SA011631.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually -- and I think 1632, excuse me, and in English at page 58. And there Dr. Karadzic says, and it may help you to identify that passage quickly, "something tells me that Mr. Krajisnik is going to conclude the proceedings soon, so I would like to make two requests. The first request is addressed to Krajina deputies. I am asking them to work a lot with our people there, with party membership, to explain our strategic goals and to explain our tactics on a daily basis." And that would be one of the reactions of the deputies in 1991 and 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you referring to the strategic goals that are an object here or our general aims, our policies? This was at a session of the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I realise the strategic goals were initially articulated in that formal way in the 16th Session. I'm not addressing myself to the strategic goals discussed on May 12th at the moment. I simply want to confirm that Dr. Karadzic told the deputies that one of their roles was to explain the goals and tactics of the Bosnian Serbs to people in the field, to the party membership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But excuse me, which session is this? Is it the one of the 15th of February? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is the 15th of February, [indiscernible] session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said that he is referring to the strategic goals of the party, whereas the 16th Session of the 12th of May was the Assembly session at which the six strategic goals were enumerated. So is your question about continuity between these goals?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, again I will ask you to listen to my question rather than concern yourself about its potential implications. I'm simply directing myself to the role of the deputies, as instructed by Dr. Karadzic on February 15th, 1992, and that was, at least in part, to explain the goals and tactics of the party and of the leadership to the party membership. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, Mr. Karadzic spoke about the policy of the party, and it's true, you're right, he was saying what our strategic goals were. I'll ask you one thing, please. When I don't understand your question, then I ask you. I'll be as expeditious as I can, but if you only tell me what you are alluding to. I couldn't make a link between these two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I had asked you about Goran Zekic, one of those deputies whose responsibility it was to explain the tactics and goals. And if you could turn to the 11th Session, please. And that's page 46 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, SA02-5757, and page 33 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I cannot find my way. I don't have it here. Can somebody help me with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, to be fair, did say something in his own language which wasn't translated and I think -- I am told by one of our team he said: Is it in the binder?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry, they did not hear the comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters have not heard it, but let's just go on the basis of the assumption that Mr. Krajisnik said such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can assure the Court he said something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a session held on --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to ask you to give me time to find the session, and I'll give you an answer straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that usually you would know what documents you would like to address the attention of Mr. Krajisnik to in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a general matter, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd like to have one copy to be prepared which in sequential order gives green or blue or red tabs like these kind of things so that we don't have to spend one minute again and again on finding the right pages. And if you would put that tab not only on the relevant document, but even already on the relevant page, and then we could certainly work far more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, thank you. And we will attend to that at the first opportunity we get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, have you found the 11th Session, and in particular have you found page 46 of the B/C/S? It's a short address by --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Zekic. And in the second paragraph before he concludes he says the following, referring to ongoing discussions. "The arrangement will never happen, and with their birth rate they will gradually stifle our territories, too, and we shall find ourselves in a difficult situation." Mr. Krajisnik, that's an expression of concern that the Muslim birth rate --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, it appears that there was some difficulty with the Court finding that particular part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was on page 33 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, page 33, three paragraphs from the bottom and two paragraphs from Mr. Zekic's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page -- [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which exhibit number are we working from, Mr. -- Because it seems that we don't have Mr. Zekic speaking on the bottom of page 33. Yes, I take it that it's page 32 -- yes, semi-last paragraph. Is it the paragraph starting: "All negotiations will continue"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 32. But here again we're working from different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document, Your Honour, is SA02-5710 through SA02-5780, which is P65 Treanor 10 tab 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a set of documents in which the actual version used appears in the -- appears in the index in bold. What I would like to be done is that we are working from one and the same document. So therefore, I don't know whether this is the same -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so everybody knows what everybody's got, I've got the same one that Your Honours have, and that's the hyper-linked one that we were using during the evidence in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm trying to consult with my legal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I was trying to be helpful, Your Honour. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties will be provided with the index of the document we are working with, which gives in bold the -- the version that is copied for us. So we have in our binders. And the parties are invited to follow that list with -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. With respect to this particular session, I note a problem that we have seen before and it may be specific to this session, it may be true of a couple of others as well, and that is there are, essentially, two cover pages. My recollection is that in one of the copies only one of the covers was copied, changing the sequence by one page or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember that we had this specific problem in relation to one of them, therefore, most likely, this one. All right. Therefore we will always deduct one page from your number being, but nevertheless you will be provided for future events and check whether the version you're working from is the same one as put in bold in our list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I believe I had asked you, looking at Mr. Zekic's comments, whether that was in fact an expression of concern about the effect, the perceived effect, of the Muslim birth rate on Bosnian Serbs within Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is that with their increasing birth rate Muslims would gradually stifle out territories and, therefore, the Serbs would be in a difficult position. That's what he was saying. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the context is very important, why he is saying this, and I would like to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- we've had a long time to talk about context, Mr. Krajisnik. We know this occurred on March 18th. We'll be talking about the period of March and the Cutileiro discussions. I presume that's the context to which you want to draw our attention, so unless it's something other than the status of discussions with the Muslims and Croats and the international community, I prefer to move on to the extent to which the Bosnian Serbs were concerned with and focussing on the Muslim birth rate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's a fair balance to be achieved here. The Defence would entirely accept that Mr. Krajisnik should not be allowed a wide-ranging exploration of other issues in the case; on the other hand, he should be allowed in the normal way to give a supplementary explanation of a succinct answer because witnesses are encouraged to give a short answer on the understanding that they will be able to expand with some explanation. There is a balance to be achieved, Your Honour, but not simply to shut him out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the question you've put to Mr. Krajisnik only was whether this was what Mr. Zekic said. Well, that's, as a matter of fact seeking verification of the correctness of the transcript of this session, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I asked -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting the Court. I think I asked whether that was an expression of concern of the potential consequences of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just have a look. You started saying: I believe I had asked you whether that was, in fact, an expression of concern. And then you continued and the end of your question you said: That's what he was saying. Right? And then you repeated the language Mr. Zekic used on paper, so finally -- your real question finally was whether that was what he said, which of course the Chamber can read unless there's any specific reason to assume that in this respect the transcript is not correctly reflecting what has been said, but I don't think that you were seeking to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps the Court will permit me to rephrase the question and then clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the other issue remains whether Mr. Krajisnik should be allowed -- Mr. Krajisnik, if such a question is asked to you, we'll allow you in one or two lines to say, yes, but you should consider this in the context of -- well, let's say the specific question of the North East of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Zekic came from the north-east, so we do allow you to add comment if you think it's of importance. We do not allow you to start a long a long story. So we allow you to explain the comment in one or two lines. You're allowed to draw our attention to some specific contextual issue that is drawn by the answer. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in fact the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Bosnian Serb deputies were concerned that -- about being overwhelmed by Muslims based, at least in part, on their -- on the perception that they had a high birth rate - isn't that right - that was the essence of concern about the birth rate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in what sense no, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No because the Muslim birth rate never bothered the Serbs for the sake of the birth rate; that is a private matter for every individual and for every nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can all accept that. What the Bosnian Serbs were concerned with was that the birth rate would lead to too many Muslims within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's it in a nutshell, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The essence is different and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to find out. The birth rate changes the balance between the several ethnicities or nationalities. That has its consequences in terms of numbers of voters stemming from that nationality. Is that what finally was of concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That did not concern the Serbs. There was something else that concerned the Serbs, and can I explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Not too long. Really, try to be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'll try. The Serbs were worried because the Muslim side advocated a unitary Bosnia, and they gave up on the agreement reached. And within a unitary Bosnia, one man would have one vote. And already they started behaving in an unconstitutional manner, and by having a majority they would simply seal off the Serbs in Bosnia. The Serbs did not complain even before because there were more Muslims, no way. So that was the reason. It's not the birth rate, it's not the fact that there are more Muslims, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Just for my -- just for your guidance, Mr. Krajisnik, listening to your answer, which certainly took more than two lines, what you could have said is that we were concerned about this, also in view of the tendency of the Muslims to act unconstitutionally. Because all the remainder what was said by you that the one man/one vote is confirmed by you. Mr. Tieger hinted at that, I hinted to the same, but you want to specifically add to that that where the Muslims were inclined to behave or had shown, as you said, to behave unconstitutionally, that that was making it a real concern. So you could have limited to that aspect, at least if I understood you well. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd have to be as wise as a Judge in order to be able to give that kind of a short answer. I'm trying to be as brief as possible. I do apologise, indeed, but I'm just trying to be helpful, to help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The perceived Muslim birth rate would lead to an increase in the number of Muslims and an increase in the number of Muslims constituted, in the eyes of the Bosnian Serbs, a threat to their living space. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and can I explain why it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well first, Mr. Krajisnik, do you recall hearing in 1991 or 1992 expressions of concern about the threat represented by Muslims to Bosnian Serb living space?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the moving in of the Muslims that was a threat in this space and building without building permits. It was the unconstitutional behaviour of the Muslims caused concern, not the fact that there were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's separate that then. It is true that the Bosnian Serbs were concerned about threats to their living space, regardless of whether it was attributable to the increase in Muslims through their birth rate or the increase in Muslims through immigration or the influx of people from outside?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were only concerned because of the immigration and because of the unlawful behaviour, nothing else, of the Muslims that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And part of that concern was the perception that Bosnian Serb living space was jeopardised. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, it was the survival of the Serbs in general that was under threat, not the space. There was a lot of space, even more than necessary. It was human rights that were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say the survival of the Serbs, you mean the biological, physical survival of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Quite simply, you have a will imposed on you that violates your national interests, if somebody had a majority in that way and behaves unconstitutionally that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to a couple of comments made in 1991 and 1992 in your presence to the living space of the Bosnian Serbs. First in the binder with Assembly sessions 1 through 7, if you could turn to the 3rd Assembly Session. And please turn to -- please turn to page 39 and 40 of the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, page 27 of the English. Excuse me, page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Kupresanin, one of the regional leaders in the Krajina, speaking. He begins his comments at the top by saying that he absolutely agrees that we should proceed with separating Serb territories. And then he continues at the seventh small paragraph, they're short paragraphs, sir, saying: "I personally think that our living space and the territory in which we live and work is endangered and we have to avert that danger, actually we have to prevent Muslims from moving into our territories and regions."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court's having any trouble finding that, I believe the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have no trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you before -- also to look at the 5th Assembly Session, as long as we're in that binder, page 41 of the B/C/S and page 43 of the English. This is a session held on 9 January 1992, where the state was proclaimed, and reflects the comments at that portion of Mr. Cancar saying: "This is the final democratic human and legal measure and possibility for the Serbian people to be on the upper-most plain of its national being, so that its living space may not shrink and the borders in which we live may not be smaller than those within which we die."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me what paragraph that is? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 41? Yes, yes, I'm sorry, I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It starts in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, essentially, Mr. Krajisnik, in those comments Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Cancar were expressing the concern that the -- that Muslims jeopardised those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were considered Bosnian Serb living space. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin is saying because they were moving in, and that's correct. And in the first paragraph he says that we have a large territory, and that's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time, and since the Court was urging us -- anyway, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until five minutes to 1.00, and I'd like to be provided with a B/C/S copy of these minutes as well so that we don't lose unnecessary time. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, one of the things that Bosnian Serbs expressed concern about and professed fear about Muslims in 1991, 1992, and indeed afterwards, was that the Muslims were allegedly going to set up an Islamic state. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individuals who spoke in this manner; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, indeed, some of those people spoke about that possibility in very striking and strident terms - isn't that correct - and charged that that was a real possibility about which the Bosnian Serbs had to be afraid?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number of people spoke in a way that was out of place and hard-line. You're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when those people spoke it -- well, first of all, did you share the hard-line views about that subject?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify a little? What are you referring to in particular, in order to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I thought we were both speaking about the allegations that Muslims were about to establish -- or intent on establishing an Islamic state. And you said that there were certain people who spoke about it in a way that was out of place and hard-line, so I assumed that you had a notion of what that was. So did you consider that some allegations about the establishment of an Islamic state were not hard-line and some were hard-line; and if so, what's the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people used derogatory names such as balija, Turks, they'll shake in their pants, things like that, because Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's Islamic declaration had been published and they were referring to that. I did not share those opinions nor did I use that vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever use the term "Turks" in referring to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did I use it, except in one conversation by telephone which somebody misinterpreted, but it was not my vocabulary. I always said that they had a right to be Muslims, and I would defend that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask to have the portion of the 33rd Assembly Session distributed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you'll see in this small packet of materials, Mr. Krajisnik, the comments of Mr. Kupresanin followed by yourself. The English part --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm moving too quickly, Your Honour. The relevant English part is found on page 66 of the English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that's a speech or comments by you, Mr. Krajisnik, which begin: "Since Vojo Kupresanin has asked me this question, I believe we have to understand something, we have strategic goals," et cetera. And then further on in that passage at the second paragraph you say: "If you want to put it like that, a half of my village is in Turk's hands. They've come to a hundred metres from my house." Now, I take it that's not an expression -- that's not a reference to Turks from Istanbul, that's a reference to Bosnian Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You are right. I don't know if ever I used such a word, but I did use it here speaking about the Muslims in a derogatory manner. I was embittered because they had taken my village. I had forgotten that. But yes, you are right, they had taken half of Zabrdje and that is what I said. I was thinking of another instance. There was a telephone conversation, but I don't recall having said that. However, I believe it's correct, although I never normally used such a term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we talked a moment ago about hard-line statements, and you asked me what I meant. So let me ask you this question: Would you consider a comment before the Assembly along the lines of the Muslims and Croats -- referring to them as the two-headed dragon, and then observing that "they want to have us imprisoned in the dark realm of Islam in the sheepholds where there is no -- there cannot be place for the peoples and historical culture and nation-building qualities." Would that be a comment of the type that you had in mind when you were referring to hard-line and inappropriate comments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what I said "in Turk's hands" is inappropriate and what they were doing there. This is not a comparison to the Turks. It would be an honour for any Muslim to be compared to the Turks, but they were calling us Chetniks. What you said is not derogatory; it's wartime vocabulary, which is bitter, and people said all sorts of things that I disagreed with. I never said anything derogatory about them, but what I said about Turks, I'm -- I've seen this for the first time now, that I said that, actually, and I think it would be a bad thing for people to use that vocabulary in public. Just as they say "Chetnik," that's derogatory, too, and I think that's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask you: Is the position of the Prosecution that Mr. Krajisnik usually used these words or that occasionally in relation to his own home village he may have done so? I mean, we spent a lot of time on something where I did not gain the impression, until now, that apart from some other words Mr. Krajisnik may have used during telephone conversations, which we would call not parliamentary expressions. What are we listening to? To occasionally using strong word or are we -- or is it more? If it's more, then please spend your time on it as you wish, but of course just as I said to the Defence that they should prioritise, the same is true for you. We have limited time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I directed your attention to a particular comment about the two-headed dragon and being imprisoned in the dark realm of Islam. So perhaps we can turn to the 24th Session at page 32 of the English, and look at the comments of Mr. Bulatovic for a moment, which I referred to. And that will be -- that's contained at page 26 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24th Session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that may need to be distributed, Mr. Krajisnik. Beginning at the bottom of page 32 of the English, and as I indicated on page 26 of the B/C/S, Mr. Kovacevic says: "The two-headed dragon has opened his jaws over the Serb people in order to swallow it, to destroy it, to wipe it off the face of the earth. Both heads, the Islamic one as well as the Vatican one are equally dangerous for us, all those democracies and democratic principles of Europe and those who find it acceptable want to push us into Alija's democratic state to have us imprisoned in the dark realm of Islam where in the sheepholds where there is no -- there cannot and must not be placed, but the people and nations of the historical cultural and nations-building." Now, would you consider that to fall within the category of hard-line statements of the intention of the Muslims to form an Islamic state or one of the more moderate professions about that intention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a moderate profession. I can only give you the context and explain why he said this. I do not agree with this sort of description.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you didn't agree with it, why did you comment immediately after Mr. Kovacevic's remarks: "I have to conclude that you are the best when you have opponents. Now Europe is the best inspiration. Thanks to Mr. Kovacevic for this speech"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I explain why I said this? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like you to explain how that's consistent with your position that you disapproved of this language and thought it inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a wonderful speaker from Herzegovina who enchanted people with his wonderful speeches. I knew every deputy well and what he thought. I wanted to soften, to mitigate his discussion, by telling him he was a good speaker in order to scatter ashes on all this. The point of the discussion was something quite different, and this was just an aside, his personal opinion. And had I told him he was in the wrong, we would not have come to our goal. So this does not constitute approval; on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say earlier that you did not claim -- that you yourself did not claim that the Muslims were trying to establish an Islamic state, that it was others who were making that claim?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the Muslims wanted to create a state in which they would dominate. Dominate. And this would be under the auspices of a civil state without three constituent units, and the principal would be one man/one vote. In that case all of Bosnia would fall under Muslim power. You can call it a Muslim state or whatever you like, but that's how it was and that was my opinion when they went back on the fundamental agreement. And they still want to do this. Under the mask of a civil state, what they really want to do is create a Muslim state and that's what the Muslim leadership wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "a Muslim state," you don't mean a state in which the Muslims were a majority, you mean an Islamic state. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean that those Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who have nothing to do with the kind of radical Islam that exists in the east, wanted their nation to be dominant and their state -- the state to be dominated by them. These are gentle people, very different from the ones we see on television in the Middle East, but they wanted this to be their state and they wanted to dominate in it, and they still want to do that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So now we go full -- come full circle and come back to my question. I think we all understand the effect of majoritarian rule in a unitary state with one man/one vote, which I think is essentially what you explained to us. My question is whether you were among those who in 1991, 1992, 1993 claimed that -- and that what the Muslims wanted, in fact, was the establishment of an Islamic state.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that they wanted to create a Muslim state. I don't exclude the possibility that I used the word "Islamic." What is certain is they wanted their own Muslim state. We have a hundred pieces of evidence to prove this. They wanted all of Bosnia or at least part of it. If I use the word "Islamic," that was because I was referring to the Islamic declaration of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, although I don't believe I used that term. But if I did, what I actually meant was a Muslim state. They wanted to have their own state and they still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a quick look at tab 14, if we can then. It's page 7 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. That's an interview with you, Dr. Karadzic, and -- well, by Risto Djogo and you and Dr. Karadzic in 1993. And during the interview you say the following: "The dominant current and the one enjoying greater support is the Sandzak one, as we call it. They are the ones who started this war and forced the Muslim people, if we can call them that, into a desperate situation where we have to fight for mere survival and who continue encouraged by fundamentalists from the east and aided by the West to try using primitive tactics cunning get tactics which is unattainable, an Islamic state within the existing state." So that's one occasion, Mr. Krajisnik, where you alleged that it was the intention of the Muslim leadership to establish an Islamic state.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part of the Muslim leadership, those people from Sandzak, yes, that's correct. Mr. Filipovic said the same in his book. You can find it there, but not Mr. Izetbegovic. However, he had to appease that arrogant majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't see that distinction being made here and I don't see that distinction being made on February 28th, 1992, when you address the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if that could be distributed if that's not available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to comment on this? I don't know if I was sufficiently clear. Should I comment on what you asked me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would suggest you wait until we address a related subject in the next document. That's a relatively short document, and on page 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the top of the document it says: "Addressed to the so-called Assembly of the Serbian People." You introduced it as the Deputies' Club. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection is we've referred to that -- it has been identified to by the -- I'll double-check, but I think throughout the course of the case that has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may well be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the understanding of this and related documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So turn to page 5 of the English. It's a very -- it's almost the end of your comments, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the portion just above the last paragraph on page 03617692. And there you say: "We are telling you what they really want. They want the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they want the currency, they want a unitary BH, they want an Islamic state." And you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's another occasion on which you advised and told the deputies of the Bosnian Serb Assembly that what the Muslims wanted to establish was an Islamic state. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are negotiations at Cutileiro's, and we are now providing information on what the others wanted in our estimation. I was saying what some of the negotiators had said. This wasn't a reference to all of them, just some of the negotiators. I didn't want to be a member of this negotiating team; you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which negotiators said that the Bosnian Muslims wanted to establish an Islamic state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the negotiations among the three parties when we were discussing, we sensed that somebody wanted to create an Islamic state. I'll give you an example. They said: What shall we do about the return of the people who left Bosnia once? And they were referring to 8 million Muslims who went to Turkey about legislation and so on. So these were negotiators; it wasn't that it was their standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think that's what I tried to ask you in the first place, Mr. Krajisnik, whether you were one of the people who claimed and told others that the Bosnian Muslims wanted to establish an Islamic state, and that is one example of that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't saying that. I was just saying what the impressions from the meeting had been, and I wasn't referring to Izetbegovic but to the people from Sandzak. If you go back to the first one, you'll see, and there were different people who were saying the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, the dispute with the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia was characterised by the Bosnian Serbs as essentially a battle with their traditional enemies.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some people spoke in those terms. Some did, not everybody. They were denying the Muslim nation and they were attributing to it a continuity with the Turk occupiers in history and also the Muslims in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, the Muslims were considered to be not only historical but perfidious enemies, cunning enemies who threatened the Serbs and had done so historically.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell us at what time and then I'll give you my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's begin with the period that we've been talking about 1991, 1992, and on, so I'm talking about the time immediately preceding and shortly after the outbreak of the conflict and extending into the conflict. Or did there come a time in your view when the Muslims began to be considered cunning, historical, and perfidious enemies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last is true, and I'll explain why. Up to the time when the government was constituted, we had been partners, respected each other. And until the declaration was made by force, we were respected. However, when the crisis broke out people began to speak in the way you are describing. When there was no agreement, the rhetoric changed. It was rhetoric, but there were people who did think that. During the war they constantly thought of the Muslims and the Croats as enemies, and they thought of us in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the Muslims and Croats, as tensions increased, were seen as historical enemies who threatened to enslave, subjugate, and even destroy the Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's leave the Croats aside. The Muslims -- well, in terms of rhetoric, Serbs were saying that they were historic enemies, and they were saying things like that when there was a crisis. Once the crisis would be over, the rhetoric would change. Now, what they thought was a different matter, so this came and went in waves. I'm talking about public statements, things that the public was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the rhetoric was either for the purpose of expressing their views or for the purpose of convincing others to share that view or both. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on who was speaking. I think that the rhetoric was understood as a democratic right, that every speaker can say what he thought. At that point of time, a time of crisis, about a certain phenomena or a certain people. So they thought no one could deny them the right to say what they thought. In a closed session it was considered as if they had said nothing at all, I mean if the media were not covering this, but there were media broadcasts. There were MPs in the joint Assembly who were saying that against the Muslims. You can find that in the stenographic notes of the joint sessions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the other way around, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. And there's no question when Bosnian Serb deputies and Bosnian Serb leaders told other representatives of the Serb people or the Serb people directly, that the Muslims would enslave them or subjugate them, or that Serbs were again facing genocide, that they were doing so for the purpose of telling them how they should respond to this dispute with the Muslims. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not right, absolutely not right. Because in any crisis the generally accepted view was the one that you heard from one side and the second side and the third side. So no one needed to be told anything. The evil genie got out of the lamp once the crisis broke out. You didn't have to persuade anybody of anything; everybody already thought the other side were their enemies, when there would be a crisis, a moment of crisis, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when Rabija Subic said at the 4th Session, "We're threatened by the same enemies again," and Mr. Zekic said at the same session, "our ranks were depopulated by genocide thanks to the certain enemies of ours that have arisen again." And Dr. Karadzic said that "the Muslims at the 5th Session were preparing laws to subjugate us, wasn't that all for the purpose of convincing everyone that a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be accepted no matter what? And that whatever had to be done to prevent it should be done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conclusion is absolutely wrong. Let me explain. Rabija Subic is a Muslim married to a Serb, in all fairness. She was saying what she thought. She was not a member of the SDS, she was a member of a different party. Mr. Karadzic spoke about the Muslims giving up on something that we had agreed upon because they want to enslave us, and that's right. They did not agree on a Bosnia consisting of three units, but they wanted a unitary Bosnia. Through the violations of the constitution, they wanted to turn us into a national minority, and that is the essence of the problem and that was correct, if somebody gives up on something once agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the bottom line of all that rhetoric, of all those expressions of positions about the threat of being enslaved and so on was that Serbs could not live with Muslims. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll tell you why the answer is no. On the 14th of October, a law was passed by force, that is to say apart from the constitution, that is to say on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Muslims said that they did not want to take into account our view. In September a decision was reached that nobody would impose any solutions on anyone; that was in 1992. And only a month later, they impose a solution. So the normal response is: If you are imposing a solution now, that means that you don't want to live with us. We are just interpreting what we saw on the spot. It's not the Serbs who made the first move, it was the Muslims and the Croats. If we didn't want to live with Muslims and Croats, we would not have accepted Bosnia and we would not have said that all three peoples were equitable. They didn't want to stay with the Serbs because they said they could not live with the Serbs in Yugoslavia. Those are the facts. That's what the Muslims said, and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, irrespective of what you consider made the first move, Mr. Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb deputies and the Bosnian Serb people were told by their leaders that they couldn't live with these people, they couldn't live with the Muslims. Isn't that the bottom line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is what the essence is: If the Muslims do not want to live with us in Yugoslavia, if they want to impose a unitary Bosnia on us in an unconstitutional way, then we are rightfully afraid to live with them in a sealed-off Bosnia-Herzegovina where they are dominant. That is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On February 28th, the same Deputies' Club, Dr. Karadzic -- and let me put this February 28th in context, as you recall. That was a session at which there was a lot of discussion about the concern that the Autonomous Region of Krajina, about the ARK, unifying with the RSK. And Dr. Karadzic spoke about the potential consequences of what he considered to be a stupid move and what he, and you, opposed. And what he said was: "Imagine the stupidity of it. The conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples, just as it was the case between India and pack Stan, that's nothing new, it resulted in a huge resettlement of the people. Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear with that. They could not live with the Hindus who are peaceful as sheep, that's the Indian religion, they couldn't live with them. They couldn't live with the Greeks on Cyprus, they couldn't live with the Arabs of Lebanon of the same language, same faith, there can be no discussion here, and yet they set up the Bosnian Krajina, and yet in two years' time you have problems again because they are overwhelm you with their birth rate and their tricks. We cannot allow that to happen." Now, that's a clear expression to the Bosnian Serb deputies who were supposed to get that message to the party membership and the Bosnian Serb people that Serbs couldn't live with Muslims. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to explain this, I assume. You don't want me to repeat the quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like you first to answer the question before you try to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's correct. I can believe that it was written that way, but let me explain that that was what the position was and I'll tell you why. Mr. Karadzic, that is to say not to have a unification of the two Krajinas, why he mentioned India, Pakistan, all of that, I'll explain all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the first question is the what question, and then only comes the why question. The what is, and that is a question put to you. Mr. Tieger asked you whether this is a clear expression to the deputies, who was supposed to pass this message to the party membership and the people, that Serbs couldn't live with Muslims. Is it that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not right and I want to explain why it's not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question is that. Tell us not why he said it but where the language seems to be relatively clear, why it is not what it seems to be at first sight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, because he said that the Muslims didn't want to live with the Serbs, because they didn't want to stay in Yugoslavia with the Serbs; that's as far as the Muslims go. But I can explain the point of it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so but keep it concise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Vance Plan envisaged some regions for the Serb people, that is to say the UNPAs, and Croatia was treated in a different way. We had our own plan, and we wanted that to be carried through, and that is the Lisbon-Sarajevo agreement. And now the people from the two Krajinas meet and what they want to do is to break-up Bosnia and Croatia. And Karadzic says: That is crazy. And of course he is using different words in order to persuade them the basic point, and that is to say not to have this unification, because in that way we would be the ones who are breaking up Bosnia. So that was the point. And we prevented that because they wanted to unite, the late Milan Babic and the others, and we did it with such great difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, if Serbs can't live with Muslims, then, insofar as possible, the territory on which -- the territories of Serbs should be pure. And that's exactly what you said on February 28th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn -- okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps let me just explain. This here is the adoption of the Sarajevo agreement, and in it we clearly stated that we want to live with the Muslims on the 28th of February. Find it and you'll see. Three constituent units. Karadzic fought against another hasty move, the unification of the two Krajinas, and he resorted to different devices in order to say this. The Muslims didn't want to live with Serbs in Yugoslavia, and that is why he said that the Serbs couldn't live with the Muslims. If they cannot live with us, how can we live with them? And they want a unitary Bosnia. Well, quite simply, he wanted to persuade them as far as this main thing is concerned, not for the two Krajinas to unite. So this is on the occasion of the Lisbon agreement. We said we wanted to live together about the Muslims in a single state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, these pure territories. Can I explain these pure territories?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do it in one minute, then do so, otherwise we'll have to wait until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than a minute, less than a minute. I thought that when the map was being drawn there should be as many Serb territories as possible according to the principle envisaged by the Lisbon Agreement. Not to be megalomaniacs and demand areas where the Serbs did not have a majority. That was all of my philosophy. That was a reference to the Lisbon Agreement. Not any kind of ethnic cleansing or anything else. Mr. Prosecutor, that is the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I got the message from the Court's last comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Tomorrow is a new day. Before we adjourn and before I instruct you, Mr. Krajisnik, not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given, I'd like to deal with one matter. The Chamber is a bit concerned about all the translations which may still have to be produced. The Chamber also, in the existing translations, including the statement of -- which I would not call yet a 92 bis statement, but at least a statement, a written statement given by Mr. Krajisnik, we would like to -- and the Chamber would also actively be involved in that to see whether that translation which is not a CLSS translation or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would like you to disclose it as soon as possible, that is still today, to the Prosecution, also to the Chamber, so that we can have a look at least on whether it's material that can be used at all at this moment on the basis of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it not before she with respect, would it not be better for -- well, it doesn't matter, Your Honour. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you could please make a copy and give it even today because we are, of course, running out of time, all of us, to both Prosecution and to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just ask, I'm wondering, Your Honour, what status it will have if we do not elect to put it in under 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik said he wanted to tender it. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In what way -- yes, well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He offered it to the Chamber. The Chamber will have a look whether it's material that could be accepted in accordance with this offer. It's happened before. We've now and then had witnesses who said: I've brought this or that and the Chamber said: We'll have a look at it and see whether it's material that could be -- that could be admitted or accepted into evidence, then whether it's Defence tendered or Prosecution tendered or Chamber-called evidence is another matter to decide. First of all, we need to know what it is, whether it is in a format to make it accessible at all to us. So therefore, you're invited to give a copy to Defence and to the legal staff of the Chamber even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, may I just say, Your Honour, Mr. Josse and I have we have considered some of these issues before. We would, in a sense, like to reserve our position because we'd really like to consider a whole lot of aspects of how various bits and pieces are dealt with and what their status is, but I won't take time today, Your Honour, but it's a general reservation of concerns of our position in relation to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Stewart, and at the same time to say the unorthodox way of introducing all this material creates problems for the Chamber as well and we have to find practical solutions for that. And this does not mean that at a later stage you would be in a position to say: For this and this reason, although offered by a witness the Defence would not want to be the party who supports or introduces this material in evidence, and you could even consider your position when the Chamber would like to have this material available as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think also, Your Honour, that's absolutely right, Your Honour. Defence counsel's concerns probably stem from the fact that Defence counsel made very little contribution to the adoption of unorthodox ways of introducing material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm not blaming you for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand it's not blame, Your Honour, in the least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's expected to be disclosed to Prosecution and legal staff of the Chamber this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I wish to mention one thing. The very last answer Mr. Krajisnik gave today is going to have to be reviewed in the morning. Mr. Sladojevic tells me there is a translation difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have even some 18 hours to what was said originally and how it appears in translation. We'll hear from you tomorrow if there's any need for correction. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, same courtroom, 9.00, and I announce to the parties that on Wednesday we'll stop a little bit earlier because there is a bureau meeting, so 20 minutes earlier than usual on next Wednesday -- this Wednesday. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of May, 2006, at 10.00 a.m.
